news.2026-11-20-sanofi-insmed-rachat.tit: Sanofi considers buying US-based Insmed, valued at more than $26 billion: the target's shares jump 17% on Wall Street
news.2026-11-20-sanofi-insmed-rachat.sum: On Thursday, November 19, Bloomberg reported that France's Sanofi is studying a takeover of Insmed, a US drugmaker specializing in respiratory diseases. Insmed shares jumped about 17% in New York, lifting its value above $26 billion. Sanofi is looking for a successor to Dupixent, its star drug [1][2][5].
news.2026-11-20-sanofi-insmed-rachat.poi: According to Bloomberg, cited by Reuters, Sanofi is working with advisers on a possible offer for Insmed. Talks are ongoing and a deal could still take several weeks; there is no guarantee it will happen, and other bidders could emerge [1][3][5].
Sanofi said it does not comment on market rumors; Insmed did not comment either [1][3].

Insmed shares gained 17% to $140.25, and trading was briefly halted by a circuit breaker, an automatic mechanism that stops trading when a price moves too fast. Its market value reached about $26.28 billion, according to LSEG data [2]. Other readings showed a gain of more than 18% [6].
The 25 analysts who cover Insmed have an average (median) target of $195 per share, well above the current price [2].
Sanofi's New York-listed shares fell 2.05% to $46.15, according to Benzinga [5].

If the deal goes ahead, it could be the biggest acquisition in the global pharmaceutical industry since Pfizer bought Seagen for $43 billion in late 2023, according to Bloomberg cited by Benzinga [5].
Insmed owns Brinsupri, a treatment that the trade site Fierce Pharma describes as a future “blockbuster,” meaning a drug that brings in more than $1 billion a year [4].
news.2026-11-20-sanofi-insmed-rachat.why: Key takeaway: Sanofi relies heavily on Dupixent, its star drug, which it developed with US-based Regeneron. Its patents expire in the early 2030s [5]. After that, cheaper copies will arrive and its sales will fall. Sanofi therefore needs to find new hit drugs now.
Buying a company that already has a promising product is faster than discovering one yourself, in your own labs. That is the path being explored by Belén Garijo, Sanofi's new CEO [5].

The stock market reaction is typical: the target's shares rise, because the buyer will have to pay a “premium,” a price above the market price, to convince shareholders to sell. The buyer's shares fall slightly, because investors fear it will overpay [2][5].
For France, it is also a sign: one of the largest groups in the CAC 40 is looking to the United States for growth, where many innovative drugmakers are based.
news.2026-11-20-sanofi-insmed-rachat.for: Sanofi is one of the biggest stocks on the Paris Bourse: if you have a PEA, an equity-based life insurance policy or an employee savings plan, you probably own a little of it. A takeover of this size could weigh on its shares in the short term, but the goal is to secure its revenue after Dupixent.

news.2026-11-20-sanofi-insmed-rachat.dee: How it works: why a target's shares jump as soon as the rumor breaks

When a company buys another listed company, it generally has to offer more than the current share price: this is the control premium. As soon as a serious rumor comes out, investors buy the target's shares, betting on this premium: the price rises even before any official offer. That is what is happening to Insmed, up 17% on Thursday [2]. The risk is that the deal does not happen: the price can then fall back. For the buyer, it is the opposite: its shares often fall slightly, like Sanofi's in New York (−2%) [5], because paying a high price raises fears of lower future profits or higher debt.

Big drugmakers pay a lot to replace drugs whose patents are about to expire.

The market criticizes Sanofi for depending on a single product: a takeover like Insmed is a response to that criticism.

news.2026-11-20-or-plus-bas-14-mois.titl: Gold falls to a 14-month low in the middle of the war with Iran: the Fed and the dollar are scarier than missiles
news.2026-11-20-or-plus-bas-14-mois.summ: Gold, the ultimate safe haven, hit its lowest level since September 2025 on Thursday, November 19, at $3,667 an ounce, and remains under pressure on Friday. The reasons: the rate hike being prepared by the US Federal Reserve and a dollar at its highest. The metal has lost more than 30% since its January record [1][2][6].
news.2026-11-20-or-plus-bas-14-mois.poin: On Thursday, an ounce of gold (31.1 grams) fell as low as $3,667.19 on the spot market, its lowest since September 2025, before trading at $3,674.13 at 8:05 p.m. Paris time, according to Reuters [2]. The December futures contract had opened Thursday at $3,730.30, down 3.2% from Wednesday's open [5].
Already on Wednesday, the December contract lost 2% to $3,789, falling below the $3,800 mark for the first time since September 2025 [3].
On Friday, Reuters confirmed that gold remains at a 14-month low, weighed down by the strong dollar and rate bets [1].

Markets see a 94% chance of a quarter-point Fed rate hike in December, and a 6% chance of a half-point hike [2]. Fed Governor Christopher Waller argued for a half-point in December or faster hikes in 2027 [2]. The Fed meeting is scheduled for December 8 and 9 [2].
The dollar hit a new 19-month high on Wednesday [2]. And the yield on 10-year US government debt is approaching its longest stretch above 5% in nearly 20 years [7].
In India, a major gold buyer, gold futures on the MCX exchange fell 3.84% on Friday to 122,561 rupees per 10 grams [8].
Key takeaway: gold pays no interest. When rates rise, a risk-free investment such as a US Treasury bond, which yields more than 5% a year [7], becomes far more attractive than a gold bar sitting in a safe. So investors sell their gold.

The dollar also plays a role: gold is bought in dollars all over the world. When the dollar rises, gold becomes more expensive for a European, Indian or Chinese buyer, who buy less of it, and its price falls [2][4].

It is a paradox: the war with Iran and the attacks around the Strait of Hormuz should push investors toward safe havens. But right now, fear of a very hawkish Fed weighs more than geopolitical fear [2][3].
The fall is all the sharper because gold had risen a lot beforehand: it has lost more than 30% since its January 2026 record [6][9]. Many investors who got in late are selling to limit their losses.
news.2026-11-20-or-plus-bas-14-mois.forM: If you own gold coins, bars or a gold fund, their value has fallen sharply this year. Conversely, if you want to buy some, it is cheaper than in January. Gold remains long-term insurance against crises, not an investment that always goes up.

news.2026-11-20-or-plus-bas-14-mois.deep: How it works: why gold falls when rates rise

Holding gold has a hidden cost: money put into a gold bar earns nothing, whereas it could earn interest elsewhere. Economists call this the opportunity cost. When the Fed raises rates, this cost increases: with a 10-year Treasury above 5% [7], holding gold means giving up 5% a year. A rate hike also draws capital to the United States, which pushes up the dollar [2]; and since gold is priced in dollars, it becomes more expensive for the rest of the world and demand falls. These two effects explain why Fed announcements sometimes matter more than wars for the price of gold [3].

Taiwan
Taiwan: TSMC's home market plunges 4.4% and heads for its worst month since 2008 as the market watchdog reins in sellers

On Thursday, November 19, the Taiex index of the Taipei stock exchange fell 1,768 points (-4.4%) to 38,426.89, its seventh-largest point drop in history. That same evening, the financial regulator tightened short-selling rules, which apply from this Friday, November 20 [1][2][3].

The Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) now bans short selling below the previous day's closing price for any stock that lost 3.5% or more in the previous session; the ban is extended by one session if the stock falls another 3.5% [2].
It also lowers the daily cap on sales of borrowed shares from 3% to 1% of average 30-day trading volume [2]. The FSC did not set an end date [2].
This is the second tightening in two weeks: on November 9, this cap had already been cut from 30% to 3%, and the collateral required from short sellers had been raised from 90% to 130% [4][5].

On Thursday, foreign investors sold 24.31 billion Taiwan dollars more in shares than they bought, according to the Taiwan Stock Exchange [1]. 1,095 stocks fell, against 71 that rose, and 128 hit their daily limit down [1].
TSMC, the world's largest contract chipmaker, lost 3.45% to 2,100 Taiwan dollars [1]. It accounts for more than 40% of the exchange's total value [1].

The decline comes from Wall Street: investors doubt the profitability of huge spending on artificial intelligence, despite Nvidia's strong results this week [1]. Already on November 16, the Taiex had fallen 6.03% [6].
According to Bloomberg, the Taiwanese market is heading for its biggest monthly drop since the 2008 financial crisis [3].

Key takeaway: Taiwan is the heart of global AI chip manufacturing, and its stock market serves as a gauge of investor sentiment on this revolution. When it plunges at this pace, it means doubts about AI are setting in [1][3].

Short selling means betting on a fall: you borrow a share, sell it, then hope to buy it back cheaper later. By limiting these sales, the regulator wants to prevent bets on a decline from accelerating the fall [2].

The method has a very recent precedent: after the first measures on November 9, the Taiex rebounded 4.94% the same day, its best session in three months [5]. But the effect did not last: the index then lost more than 5,000 points in three sessions [7].
The measures do not ban short selling: they slow it down on days of sharp declines. They do nothing about the cause, the AI fears coming from the United States [2][1].

What about me? If you have a global fund, a “tech” fund or an emerging markets fund, TSMC is often part of it, and this fall weighs on its value. Taiwanese chips are also in your phone and your computer: the health of this sector matters for the entire digital economy [1].

How it works: short selling

An investor who thinks a stock will fall can borrow it (for a small fee) from another investor, sell it immediately, then buy it back later to return it. If the price has fallen in the meantime, they pocket the difference; if it has risen, they lose. These sales amplify declines when panic sets in, because they add sellers. That is why regulators limit them during crashes: in Taiwan, short selling at a price below the previous day's close is banned for stocks that have just fallen 3.5% [2]. Critics respond that these sellers also help set a fair price, and that blocking them does not remove the cause of the decline.

news.2026-11-20-intuit-chute-ross-gap.ti: Wall Street: software maker Intuit falls 10% after its forecast and the sale of Mailchimp, Ross stores disappoint ahead of the holidays
news.2026-11-20-intuit-chute-ross-gap.su: On Thursday evening, November 19, after the close of an already grim session on Wall Street, shares of software maker Intuit lost about 10%: its sales forecast fell well short of expectations. Retail chain Ross Stores also slipped, while Gap rose thanks to better-than-expected earnings [1][2][3].
news.2026-11-20-intuit-chute-ross-gap.po: Intuit expects second-quarter revenue of $4.93 billion to $4.95 billion, while analysts were expecting $5.11 billion [3].
The group also announced an agreement to sell its Mailchimp unit [3][4].
After the close, Intuit shares fell to $279.88, down 9.7% from their close of $310.02, according to Nasdaq data; CNBC reported declines of as much as 13% in extended trading [1][3].

Ross Stores expects earnings of $2.16 to $2.25 per share for its fourth quarter, the holiday quarter, while analysts polled by LSEG expected $2.28. Its shares were down between 5% and 9% in extended trading, depending on the source [3].

Apparel group Gap earned 82 cents per share on an adjusted basis, versus 78 expected. Its shares rose about 3% in extended trading, despite a lowered annual sales forecast and a start to the holiday season held back by mild weather [3][4].

The backdrop is heavy: on Thursday, the Dow Jones lost 1,101 points (−2.19%) to 49,097 points, the Nasdaq 2.25% and the S&P 500 2.02%, its sixth straight decline. All 11 sectors of the S&P 500 ended in the red [5].
news.2026-11-20-intuit-chute-ross-gap.wh: Key takeaway: on the stock market, a company is judged on what it promises. Intuit probably did well this quarter, but it is forecasting $160 million to $180 million less in sales than analysts expected [3], and that is what is sinking the stock.

Software makers have been under pressure for weeks: investors fear that artificial intelligence will let people do for themselves, for free, what this software sells by subscription. The tech-heavy Nasdaq has in fact entered a correction, meaning a drop of more than 10% from its record [6].

Ross and Gap send another signal, on consumer spending: Americans remain on the lookout for low prices, but retailers are cautious about the holidays, the most important period of the year for them [3][4].
All this comes as the Fed, the US central bank, prepares to raise rates, making credit more expensive for households and businesses alike [5].
news.2026-11-20-intuit-chute-ross-gap.fo: These companies are not well known in France, but they carry weight in the major US indexes, and therefore in the “global” or “S&P 500” funds that are very common in PEAs and life insurance policies. A grim session in New York almost always ends up showing on your statement.

news.2026-11-20-intuit-chute-ross-gap.de: How it works: the “after-hours” market, after the close

The New York Stock Exchange closes at 4 p.m. local time (10 p.m. in Paris), but you can keep buying and selling shares for a few more hours on electronic platforms: this is the after-hours market. Many companies publish their results just after the close, to give investors time to read them. The first price moves therefore happen after hours, with few buyers and sellers, which can exaggerate them: for Intuit, readings range from −9.7% to −13% depending on the time [1][3]. The real verdict comes the next day, when the regular session opens.

news.2026-11-20-ubisoft-perte-semestre.t: Ubisoft loses €254 million in six months and cuts 1,100 jobs, on the very day GTA VI, the most anticipated game in history, comes out from its US rival
news.2026-11-20-ubisoft-perte-semestre.s: On Thursday, November 19, France's Ubisoft (Assassin's Creed) reported a net loss of €254.5 million for the first half and sales down 16.5%. The group is sticking to its targets, but its shares lost another 2% in Paris, and more than 35% since January. The same day, GTA VI from US-based Take-Two was released [1][2][3][7].
news.2026-11-20-ubisoft-perte-semestre.p: From April to September 2026, Ubisoft's net bookings, the industry's sales indicator, reached €644.7 million, compared with €772.4 million a year earlier, down 16.5% [1].
The second quarter alone reached €388.9 million (−20.8%), above the target of about €370 million, mainly thanks to Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced, a new version of an older installment [1].
Sales of older games (the “back catalog”) fell 40.8% to €438.8 million. Digital sales, downloads and in-game purchases, amounted to €548.2 million [1].

The net loss reached €254.5 million [3][4]. The operating loss widened to €189.2 million, compared with €120.2 million a year earlier, and the group burned €338.1 million in cash, compared with €250.7 million [3].
Ubisoft cut its fixed costs by 6% to €660 million and eliminated about 1,100 jobs over the half [2].
For the third quarter, it is targeting about €250 million in bookings and confirms for the fiscal year a decline “in the high single digits,” meaning just under 10% [1].
The stock closed Thursday at €4.169, down 2.07%, and is down 35.28% since the start of the year [2].
news.2026-11-20-ubisoft-perte-semestre.w: Key takeaway: Ubisoft, long the pride of the French video game industry, is selling less and less and losing a lot of money. It is cutting staff to survive, betting on its major franchises such as Assassin's Creed [1][2].

The timing is cruel: on the same day, November 19, GTA VI from US-based Take-Two was released on PS5 and Xbox [5]. According to research firm Sensor Tower, cited by Reuters, about 17.1 million copies had already been sold by noon New York time the day before [6]. A hit like this captures players' money and time for weeks.
Yet even Take-Two is not soaring: after rising about 6% on November 18 thanks to glowing reviews, its shares fell on release day [6][8]. Investors had already bet on the game's success.
news.2026-11-20-ubisoft-perte-semestre.f: If you play, expect Ubisoft to release mostly sequels and remakes of its well-known franchises, which are less risky. If you own Ubisoft shares, be aware that the stock has lost more than a third of its value this year: the promised turnaround has not yet convinced the market.

news.2026-11-20-ubisoft-perte-semestre.d: How it works: “net bookings,” the video game industry's compass

In video games, money does not come in all at once: a player buys a game, then expansions or items for months. Accounting rules therefore spread part of the revenue over time. To see what was actually sold over a period, publishers like Ubisoft report “net bookings”: everything players paid, games and in-game purchases, over the period [1]. This is the figure the stock market looks at first. Here, it is down 16.5% over six months, even though the second quarter did slightly better than the target of about €370 million [1].

news.2026-11-20-cuivre-plus-bas-7-mois.t: Copper has its worst day in 19 months and falls to a seven-month low, even as China is short of metal
news.2026-11-20-cuivre-plus-bas-7-mois.s: Copper, a key metal for electricity and data centers, fell this week to its lowest level in seven months, after its worst session in 19 months. Hedge funds are selling, worried about AI-related demand. The paradox: in Shanghai, inventories are at their lowest since 2023 [1][2][3][4].
news.2026-11-20-cuivre-plus-bas-7-mois.p: The three-month copper price on the London Metal Exchange (LME), the global benchmark, fell to around $12,400 to $12,800 a ton depending on the time, its lowest in seven months [1][2].
For the Canadian daily The Globe and Mail, it was copper's worst day in 19 months. “It looks like people are throwing in the towel,” one market participant told the paper [3].
The decline is mainly due to selling by hedge funds, which bet on short-term prices, rather than a collapse in real demand [2][4].
Sellers are worried about demand from AI data centers, big consumers of copper cables, a stronger dollar and disappointing Chinese economic data [1].

Yet in China, the metal is in short supply: inventories on the Shanghai exchange fell 18% to their lowest since December 2023, to the point that the exchange had to step in. The premium paid to import copper at the port of Yangshan hit a record $360 a ton [4].
On Thursday, copper rebounded 0.7% to $12,558 a ton, as buyers took advantage of lower prices [5].
news.2026-11-20-cuivre-plus-bas-7-mois.w: Key takeaway: the price of copper often serves as a gauge of the global economy. It is everywhere: power grids, electric cars, wind turbines and, increasingly, data centers. When it falls, it means investors see growth slowing.

This time, the fall mainly reflects the same fear that is hitting stock markets: that AI giants will spend less on their data centers [1]. It also comes from the Fed: a strong dollar makes copper, priced in dollars, more expensive for foreign buyers [1].

But the physical market tells a different story: in China, inventories are melting away and importers are paying a record price to get metal [4]. The gap between fund bets and physical need can trigger sharp rebounds, like Thursday's [5].
news.2026-11-20-cuivre-plus-bas-7-mois.f: Cheaper copper could eventually lower the cost of cables, electrical appliances or energy-efficiency renovation work a little. In India, air conditioner makers have benefited on the stock market, but cable makers risk losses on inventory bought at higher prices [6].

news.2026-11-20-cuivre-plus-bas-7-mois.d: How it works: when funds and factories tell different stories

The price of copper is set mainly on futures markets, in London, New York and Shanghai, where contracts for future delivery are bought and sold. Manufacturers use them to hedge their purchases, but hedge funds also bet there on rises or falls, without ever touching the metal. When these funds sell en masse, the price falls, even if factories still need it [2][4]. The gap shows up in other indicators: warehouse inventories and the premium paid to get the metal immediately. In China, these two signals say the opposite of the price: inventories at their lowest since 2023, a record premium [4]. If funds have to buy back, the price can rise again very quickly.

Big copper shocks often stem from fears about global growth; the price can then recover if the economy holds up.

news.2026-11-20-vie-chere-manifestations: Cost of living: unions and groups in seven European countries call for three days of protests, November 20 to 22

From this Friday, November 20, through Sunday, unions and associations in seven European countries are calling for protests against the high cost of living. The idea was born in Spain, among tenants' unions, and was decided at a meeting in Paris on November 3 [1][2].
These days of action were set on November 3 in Paris, according to AFP. The Confederation of Spanish Tenants' Unions initiated this coordination [1].
In France, the CGT, Solidaires and the housing rights association Droit au logement (DAL) support the call [2].
The demands: a “guaranteed right to housing,” price controls on housing, food and energy, public services, taxing the wealthiest, and an end to rearmament and new fossil fuel projects [1].
In Nantes, an anti-militarist protest is planned for Friday at 2 p.m., near the maritime station [3].
Key takeaway: anger over the cost of living crosses borders, and housing has become its symbol, from Madrid to Paris [1].
The movement combines two issues: purchasing power and opposition to public money going to defense, at a time when European countries are rearming [1].
If you need to travel this weekend, check which gatherings are planned in your city. On the substance, these demands (rent, energy, food) concern the expenses that weigh most on your budget.

news.2026-11-20-belgique-manifestation-n: Belgium: the three major unions call for a national demonstration in Brussels on Monday against the De Wever government's cuts

Belgian unions ACV-CSC, FGTB-ABVV and SYNOVA expect thousands of people in Brussels on Monday, November 23, for a national demonstration against cuts to the federal social budget. Disruptions are expected, but SNCB promises normal train service [1].
The three unions are organizing the demonstration against the federal government's social spending cuts [1].
“No strike notice has been filed, so our service will run normally on Monday,” said SNCB, the rail operator [1].
In early November, Prime Minister Bart De Wever had offered his resignation to King Philippe, who put it on hold, amid a budget battle [2].
The government is seeking about €10 billion in savings [2].
Key takeaway: Belgium is experiencing almost continuous social protest against austerity, with roughly one general strike a month for the past year [2].
The De Wever government wants to make savings, but every cut to the social budget revives the protests, and the budget already nearly brought down the coalition in early November [1][2].

If you are going to Brussels on Monday, expect disruptions to public transport in the city, even though national trains should run. The Belgian debate closely resembles the French one: how to reduce the deficit without breaking the social model.

news.2026-11-20-hongrie-etat-de-droit-ue: Hungary: EU ministers scrutinize the rule of law under Péter Magyar, but the Article 7 procedure remains open

On Thursday, November 19, EU ministers for European affairs reviewed Hungary, along with Cyprus, Lithuania and Luxembourg, during the annual rule-of-law dialogue. Péter Magyar's government has launched reforms, but the 2018 sanctions procedure has not been closed [1][2].
This is a regular review, not a special hearing against Budapest or a vote on sanctions, Euronews points out [1].
The ministers rely on the Commission's reports published in July [2].

The Magyar government has adopted new anti-corruption and judicial reforms, and ended government by emergency decree [1]. The Council had welcomed reforms paving the way for unfreezing some EU funds [2].
The Article 7 procedure, launched by the European Parliament in September 2018, remains open and separate from this dialogue [2][3].
Key takeaway: Péter Magyar's government has quickly reversed policies that had put Hungary at odds with the EU, but the 27 member states and the Commission continue to assess its measures [1][2].

Article 7 of the EU treaty is the procedure used when a country is suspected of threatening the EU's values. As long as it remains open, Hungary stays under watch, even if the reports become more positive [2][3].
Hungary falling back in line matters to you: it means one less veto on European decisions such as aid to Ukraine or sanctions against Russia.

news.2026-11-20-portugal-budget-monteneg: Portugal: without a majority, Prime Minister Luís Montenegro fears an “institutional deadlock” over the 2027 budget

Portuguese Prime Minister Luís Montenegro warned lawmakers from his PSD-CDS coalition that the battle over the 2027 budget could lead to an “institutional deadlock.” To the opposition, he said: “If you want to govern, come to an agreement among yourselves” [1].
Montenegro was speaking behind closed doors to the PSD and CDS parliamentary groups, according to the Lusa news agency [1].
He denounced “interference in the government's sphere” during the budget review and called the opposition's proposals incoherent [1].
His government is a minority government and believes the changes being demanded would cost too much [2].
A few days earlier, he had said that street protests, particularly over housing, could give a “bad image” of Portugal [2][3].
Key takeaway: as in France, a government without a majority must pass a budget in the face of an opposition that amends it as it pleases [1][2].
Montenegro defends his government's economic record, but anger over housing is spilling into the streets and complicating budget choices [2][3].
If you are planning to move to or buy property in Portugal, the housing crisis and budget uncertainty are two things to watch.

news.2026-11-20-mexique-sheinbaum-accord: Mexico: Sheinbaum hopes to seal a trade deal with Trump at the G20 in Miami in December

On Thursday, November 19, in Shenzhen, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said she hoped to conclude a new trade deal with Donald Trump at their next meeting, scheduled for the G20 in Miami in December. She is seeking relief from US tariffs on vehicles, steel and aluminum [1].
The two leaders met earlier in the week on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen and agreed to meet again at the G20 in Miami in December [1].
The two countries want to “determine whether an agreement is possible,” Claudia Sheinbaum said, without giving further details [1].
In July, Washington refused to extend the North American free trade agreement (USMCA) for sixteen years [1]. On November 17, Mexico City and Ottawa reaffirmed their commitment to renewing it [3].
Sheinbaum also wants stronger ties with China, without, she says, harming relations with Washington [1]. She left Shenzhen on Thursday evening after a “very productive” four-day visit [2].
Key takeaway: Mexico wants to settle tariffs on its cars, steel and aluminum through a direct deal with Trump, without waiting for the full review of the North American agreement [1].
Mexico is playing on two fronts: moving closer to China while negotiating with Washington [1].
Mexico is a major automotive workshop for the US market: a tariff deal would change costs for the carmakers that produce there, and therefore car prices.

news.2026-11-20-canada-ndrangheta-sancti: Canada: Washington sanctions the Toronto branch of the Calabrian mafia, accused of helping Mexican cartels

On Thursday, November 19, the US Treasury sanctioned the 'Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia, and its branch in the Toronto area, as well as the Comancheros motorcycle gang, which originated in Australia. Washington accuses them of helping cartels designated as “terrorist organizations,” such as the Sinaloa cartel [1][2][4].

The sanctions target six key 'Ndrangheta figures in the Toronto area, as well as the wife and children of one of the leaders, Luigi Vescio Sr., 55 [2][3]. Three funeral homes in the area, in Woodbridge, Toronto and Maple, are also targeted [3].
The Treasury names Angelo Figliomeni, known as “Don Angelino,” as head of the Toronto faction [1].
The Toronto branch is accused of laundering money through the Canadian and US financial systems and of exerting influence even over events in Italy [1][2].
According to the State Department, the two groups provide logistical support to the Sinaloa cartel, the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) and Colombia's Clan del Golfo [4].
Key takeaway: Washington is extending its war on cartels to criminal networks based in allied countries, by targeting their money [1][2].

How it works: a Treasury sanction (through its OFAC office) freezes the assets of the targeted people in the United States and bars Americans from doing business with them, which in practice cuts them off from the dollar [1].
The 'Ndrangheta is first and foremost an Italian mafia: when Washington targets its financial channels, European banks must also step up their vigilance.
news.2026-11-20-afrique-du-sud-taux-paus: South Africa: the central bank holds its rate at 7.25%, but three of seven members already wanted to raise it

On Thursday, November 19, the South African Reserve Bank left its key rate at 7.25%. The decision was very close: four committee members voted to hold, three for a hike. Inflation is picking up, and the governor speaks of a mere “pause” [1][2].
The banks' prime rate, which serves as the basis for consumer loans, remains at 10.75% [3].
Inflation rose to 5.2% in October, from 4.5% in September, driven by food and fuel [3][4].
Governor Lesetja Kganyago warned that the bank would not hesitate to raise rates if necessary [3]. The bank also fears that El Niño will push up food prices [5].
RMB bank expects a 0.25-point hike in January 2027 [3].
Key takeaway: South Africa is caught between rebounding inflation and weak growth: raising rates would slow activity further [4].
A four-to-three vote shows that a hike is close: the next committee meeting, in January, will be decisive for indebted households [2][3].
What about me? The South African rand reacts to these decisions: for a trip to South Africa or an investment in emerging markets, an upcoming rate hike could support the currency [3].

news.2026-11-20-egypte-libye-neuf-accord: Egypt-Libya: nine gas and oil agreements signed in Cairo, despite the dispute over maritime borders with Turkey

On Thursday, November 19, in Cairo, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi received Libyan Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah. The two countries signed nine agreements and protocols, from energy to fishing, even though they disagree over a maritime deal between Tripoli and Ankara [1][2].
Two framework agreements cover gas infrastructure and oil refining; they were signed by the two countries' oil ministers [2][3].
The other texts cover education, fishing and communications [2][3].

Egypt considers “null” the maritime agreement signed in 2019 between Libya and Turkey, which it says encroaches on its rights in the Mediterranean; it said so to the UN in a note dated November 5 [1].
The eastern Libyan parliament ratified this agreement on October 20; the European Union responded the very next day that it could have no legal effect on other countries [4].
Key takeaway: Egypt is moving closer to the Tripoli government, after long supporting its eastern rival, Khalifa Haftar. On November 7, it reopened its embassy in Tripoli, closed since 2014 [4].
What is at stake is the gas fields of the Eastern Mediterranean: who owns which maritime zone decides who can drill. Greece, Cyprus and Egypt contest the Turkish-Libyan agreement [4].
What about me? Libya and Egypt are gas and oil suppliers close to Europe. Their cooperation matters for Europe's energy supply, including France's [3][4].

news.2026-11-20-chine-taux-inchanges-18e: China: despite a stalling economy, Beijing leaves its lending rates unchanged for the 18th month in a row

On Friday, November 20, China kept its benchmark lending rates, the “loan prime rates,” unchanged: 3% for one year and 3.5% for five years. It is the 18th time in a row that they have not moved [1][2][3].
The one-year rate serves as the basis for loans to businesses and households, the five-year rate for mortgages [1][2].
The central bank (People's Bank of China) has changed its main tool: its overnight loans to banks, at 1.25%, have become its benchmark daily operation [2].
According to analysts, this change amounts to lowering the floor of Chinese rates by 0.15 point, without touching the published rates [2].
Citi, cited by Reuters, expects two 0.1-point cuts in 2027 [2].
Key takeaway: Beijing prefers discreet nudges, by changing tools, to a clear and visible cut in its rates [2].

The rates are announced every month by the National Interbank Funding Center [3]. Their stability for a year and a half shows that the central bank is keeping its ammunition, while analysts do not expect a cut before 2027 [2].
What about me? China is a major customer of European companies, from luxury goods to cars. If its central bank is slow to revive lending, their sales there will remain under pressure [2].
